title: These 33 Lines Cut Claude Code Token Usage by 90%
core_takeaway: A forensic teardown of Spotify's open-source Claude Code plugin ('shunt') that intercepts large file reads with a pre-tool-use hook and delegates them to a cheap Gemini-flash-tier model, returning only bullets into Claude's context. The headline '90% off Claude Code token usage' is the mean of three file-read benchmarks (82%, 94%, 94%) from a single product manager's post, not a fleet-wide engineering result, and the money saved is ~86% not 90% — though across 20 turns of cache re-sends it actually lands nearer 91% because the avoided tokens would have been re-billed every turn. The verdict: steal the 33-line bash hook, leave the cheap-model round trip.
key_points: The blog post is first-person by a principal product manager (name garbled in captions as 'Dmitri Masminoff'), and its own title says 'my token usage' — the repo's benchmark table is the real evidence and reads '82 to 94%' across three file-read scenarios; the fourth scenario, code generation, has a dash in that column.

Version one was advisory: routing rules in a markdown file saying 'use the cheap model on big files, please'. Claude could ignore them and every project needed its own copy. Version two replaced the sign with a turnstile — a hook that blocks. 'Written rules are a suggestion. A block is not.'

The read hook parses only three fields off stdin (path, offset, limit) and runs four tests, the first three of which exist to let the call through: already-sliced reads pass, empty or missing paths pass so the read tool reports its own error, and files at or under 350 lines pass because below that the detour costs more than it saves.

On a block the hook prints a refusal naming the real numbers ('this file is 602 lines, threshold 350') plus the fix ('use the bulk reader skill; re-read with an offset if you need exact content to edit'), so the instruction arrives as the result of the model's own attempt rather than sitting in a config file hoping to be remembered.

The whole gate is 33 lines of bash — no service, no proxy, no vendor, nothing in front of your traffic. A second hook closes the cat/head/tail loophole while deliberately allowing pipes (already targeted) and redirects (output never enters the conversation).

Benchmark economics: a source file plus its tests (~12,000 lines) cost Claude ~76,000 tokens to read directly versus ~4,000 for the bullets. But at $15/M for Claude's top tier vs $0.30/M for the flash tier, the ~16:1 price ratio — not the token count — is the entire economic engine; the 76,000 tokens don't vanish, someone still reads every one at 30 cents a million.

Because Claude Code caches the prefix, a read you pay for once is re-sent at a tenth of price on every subsequent turn: at 20 turns the plain version costs ~$1.14 (two-thirds of it cached re-reads) versus under 10 cents with the plugin — 91% better, so the post undersells its own mechanism. The flip side: anything that adds turns eats the saving, and a 10-30 second detour returning a distrusted summary does exactly that.

Spotify's own stated limits are what make the rest credible: you can't delegate and edit because the summaries carry no reliable line numbers, and in their testing the cheap reader missed a thread-safety bug Claude caught in seconds. Buried under 'known limitations' is 'no enforcement for codewriter' — the code-writing half of their own system relies on Claude noticing a description and choosing to comply, which contradicts their own thesis.

The strongest counter-evidence is JetBrains' RTK experiment six weeks earlier on a structurally identical hook: same 86-task suite in both arms, agent pinned to one version, four paired runs, 425 build trials, endpoints written down before any run. Advertised 60-90% savings; measured 7.6% MORE expensive per task at low reasoning effort, a coin flip at high effort, with no quality movement — because runs used ~14% more turns and ~14% more cache reads. Its own dashboard still reported '96 million tokens saved' on runs that cost more, estimating tokens by dividing characters by four.
why_it_matters: This is the clearest available case study in enforcement-as-architecture: the durable idea isn't the cheap model, it's that a hook firing at the moment of the attempt beats any rule written in an instructions file — directly applicable to any agent suite whose CLAUDE.md rules get ignored. It also hands you a reusable skepticism protocol for every 'saves N% of tokens' tool: a self-reported saving is a claim about a counterfactual, not about your bill, and the JetBrains paired-run design is the template for measuring your own. The turn-count insight (savings die when a tool adds turns) is the governing constraint for any delegation or compaction feature.
